title: Electric Field Strength: V/m, kV/mm and Dielectric Breakdown
h1: Electric field strength units — V/m and kV/mm
description: 1 kV/mm = 10⁶ V/m. Air breaks down at 3 kV/mm; PET film at 300 kV/mm; SF₆ at 89 kV/mm. Miss the unit and insulation design fails.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Field strength is what breaks down insulators. Voltage matters only in context of thickness.
body: Dielectric breakdown is a field problem, not a voltage problem. A 1 kV signal is fine on 1 mm of Mylar and catastrophic on 1 µm of the same film. Field strength captures this.

> 1 kV/mm = 10⁶ V/m = 1 MV/m
> 1 V/mil = 39.37 V/mm = 39 370 V/m
Dry air (STP): 3 kV/mm. Distilled water: ~65 kV/mm short term. Mineral oil: 12–15 kV/mm. FR-4: 20 kV/mm. Kapton: 300 kV/mm. SF₆ at 1 bar: 89 kV/mm. Vacuum: geometry-dependent, often 20 kV/mm.

A 33 kV cable with 8 mm insulation runs at 4.1 kV/mm average — well below XLPE's 50 kV/mm short-term strength, but partial discharge inception starts at 3–5 kV/mm over decades. Design margins live in the field strength number, not the voltage.
kV/mm is the language. Check both peak and continuous field strength against material limits.

faqs.a: Yes — AC breakdown is 30–70% of DC breakdown for most solids because heating and partial discharge accumulate.

faqs.q: Is 'BIL' the same as dielectric strength?
faqs.a: No — BIL (basic insulation level) is a system-level voltage rating standardised across a device, not a per-material field strength.
